name: Where Is Gilgamesh? (Kurdish: Gilgamesh le kwêye?) [uncertain: Kurdish title transliteration not verified]
date: Released 1 February 2024; shot in 2022 to 2023 after the director returned to Kurdistan in 2022 [uncertain: exact shoot dates]
creator: Karzan Kardozi (writer, director, producer, self-funded; also did post-production himself). Kurdish American filmmaker born 1983 in Sulaymaniyah, left Kurdistan in 1999, trained at Watkins College of Art, Design & Film (Nashville) and the University of Central Lancashire.
form: Feature film: Kurdish-language (Sorani) heist crime film noir, 90 minutes, a loose modern-day adaptation rather than a translation
translator_access: Not a translation. Kardozi works from the epic's narrative outline (presumably via published English or Kurdish translations) and transposes characters and episodes into a present-day crime plot; no evidence he reads Akkadian or used a scholar's crib. [uncertain]
versions_used: Draws on the overall arc of the Standard Babylonian epic (Enkidu's death, the underworld or sea-bed journey, Urshanabi) and puts the Sulaymaniyah Tablet V, the Old Babylonian-era tablet acquired by the Sulaymaniyah Museum in 2011 and published by Al-Rawi and George in 2014, at the centre as the stolen MacGuffin. The real tablet appears on screen.
non_standard_material: Silent merge. Mythic figures become modern characters with no textual apparatus: Govan (Gilgamesh), Akam (Enkidu), Avin (Inanna/Ishtar), Avin's father (Enlil), Haji Hazo (Humbaba), a truck driver in the Urshanabi role, plus an invented secret society that follows ancient Sumerian beliefs.
gap_policy: Not applicable in the textual sense; the film smooths the epic into a continuous thriller plot. The fragmentary tablet itself is the object being chased, so loss is literalised as theft rather than shown as lacunae.
typography_of_absence: None on the page. The closest equivalent is the physical tablet as a stolen, missing object, and a three-hour first cut reduced to 90 minutes because no Kurdish cinema would screen a three-hour film.
tablet_xii: Dropped as such; the underworld motif is carried instead by Govan's descent into the sewers. [uncertain]
turning_point: The death of Govan's friend Akam (the Enkidu figure) turns the heist story into a grief-driven pursuit, mirroring Enkidu's death as the epic's hinge. The descent into the sewers (Gilgamesh's underworld or sea-bed journey) and advice from a truck driver (Urshanabi) follow as the quest phase. Initial trigger is the kidnapping of Govan's mother, which forces him to steal the tablet, a twist on Ninsun petitioning Shamash for her son. [uncertain: exact ending not documented in available sources]
arc_interpretation: Reads as quest plus inner reckoning: the logline says Govan 'faces his own inner demons' while trying to recover the tablet. The epic is recast as a story about cultural heritage and loyalty, with the guard as a flawed protector who must recover what was taken from his own city. The loss of a companion and the descent motif keep grief and mortality in the frame, but the explicit stakes are recovery of the tablet and of Kurdish heritage from smugglers and a London auction. [uncertain]
key_passages: No verse passages are rendered. Parallels reported by Kurdistan Chronicle: Govan's mother seeking a talisman (Ninsun invoking the sun god), Akam's death (Enkidu), Haji Hazo as the guardian-antagonist (Humbaba), Avin as the dangerous seductive figure (Inanna/Ishtar), sewers as underworld, truck driver as Urshanabi. No specific equivalents documented for Shamhat, Siduri's advice, or the closing walls of Uruk. [uncertain]
diction_and_metre: Not verse. Modern colloquial Sorani Kurdish dialogue in a film-noir crime register.
sample_line: Logline: 'A priceless tablet of Gilgamesh, the oldest and most important work of literature, is stolen from a museum. A security guard vows to do whatever it takes to get it back from a group of smugglers.' (FilmFreeway / Kurdistan Chronicle) [uncertain: wording paraphrased in some sources]
critical_response: Little formal criticism found. Coverage is mostly regional features, notably Kurdistan Chronicle's 'The Epic of Gilgamesh Comes to the Silver Screen', which frames it as an ambitious micro-budget adaptation. IMDb user rating around 8.9 on a small vote count (tt22817100); listed on Letterboxd. No major English-language reviews or festival awards located. [uncertain]
regional_reception: Made in and about Iraqi Kurdistan, in Sorani Kurdish, shot entirely in Sulaymaniyah with scenes inside the Sulaymaniyah Museum, which holds the real Tablet V. Released in Kurdish cinemas; the running time was cut to 90 minutes specifically for local cinema exhibition. A clear case of the epic returning to its region of origin through popular genre film.
ai_craft_tension: No machine role. The film is a counterweight to AI-recovery stories: the same Tablet V that scholars joined and translated by hand is here reclaimed by storytelling in its home city. It shows what a reader-maker adds that no pipeline does: mapping Enkidu, Humbaba and Urshanabi onto a guard, a gangster and a truck driver so the story lands with a local audience. It also dramatises the provenance problem (smugglers, a London auction) that sits behind many digitised fragments.
essay_hooks: 1) Budget of $9,000, a crew of five to seven, a 29-day shoot entirely in Sulaymaniyah (Wikipedia; Kurdistan Chronicle), for a story about a tablet worth more than the film. 2) The real Tablet V appears on screen in the museum where it is held. 3) Irony worth checking: the real Sulaymaniyah tablet reached the museum in 2011 via purchase from a smuggler, and the film's plot is smugglers stealing it back for a London auction. 4) Kardozi cut a three-hour version to 90 minutes because 'no cinema in Kurdistan would run a movie that was three hours long' (Kurdistan Chronicle). 5) Gilgamesh's descent to the underworld becomes a museum guard crawling through sewers.
